picked.t: 2 central HCMC roads to become one-way from Oct 10 for metro construction
picked.body: Vu Van Vinh, director of Project Management Board 2 under the Ho Chi Minh City Management Authority for Urban Railways (MAUR), noted that work on the Ben Thanh-Tham Luong section of Metro Line 2 is underway at five underground stations: Pham Van Bach, Le Thi Rieng, Hoa Hung, Pham Van Hai, and Ba Queo. Construction at the Tao Dan and Bay Hien stations will also begin this month. To facilitate this, the municipal Department of Construction has approved a traffic management plan allowing contractors to install street barriers starting Oct. 10. Under the plan, sections of Nguyen Thi Minh Khai and Cach Mang Thang Tam will be converted to one-way traffic. The roads serve as vital links connecting the city's northwestern gateways to the downtown, and are prone to rush-hour congestion. On Cach Mang Thang Tam Street, a 350-m section between Nguyen Du and Nguyen Thi Minh Khai will carry traffic solely from Nguyen Du toward Nguyen Thi Minh Khai. Drivers heading in the opposite direction must detour via Nguyen Thi Minh Khai, Huyen Tran Cong Chua, Thu Khoa Huan, Le Thanh Ton, and Pham Hong Thai streets before reconnecting with Cach Mang Thang Tam. A 1.5-km stretch of Nguyen Thi Minh Khai will become one-way from Cao Thang toward Huyen Tran Cong Chua. Alternative routes for the opposite direction include taking Truong Dinh to Vo Van Tan, or following Nguyen Dinh Chieu to Cao Thang before returning to Nguyen Thi Minh Khai. To help ease the surrounding traffic flow, nearby Suong Nguyet Anh and Bui Thi Xuan streets near Tao Dan Station will allow two-way travel for all vehicles. Vinh stated that the underground station construction will occur in five phases over more than three years. Contractors will widen temporary roadways and install barriers in stages, ensuring at least 7.5 m of roadway remains open for vehicles. Authorities will be on-site to regulate and redirect traffic to minimize gridlock. Cach Mang Thang Tam previously restricted cars to one direction between the Bay Hien Intersection and Dan Chu Roundabout to facilitate work on the Le Thi Rieng Station. Construction on the remaining three stations, Ben Thanh, Dan Chu, and Nguyen Hong Dao, is scheduled to begin later in 2026, with traffic management plans being finalized. The Ben Thanh-Tham Luong section of Metro Line 2 broke ground on Jan. 15 with a total investment exceeding VND55 trillion (US$2.12 billion). The route spans nearly 11.3 km, including a 9.3-km underground stretch, and features 10 underground stations, one elevated station, and the Tham Luong depot. The project is slated for completion in 2030, providing a seamless transit connection between central Ho Chi Minh City and its northwestern districts.

picked.t: One reason many SMEs struggle to scale, according to business advisors
picked.body: In the early stages, SME founders are often among their companies' greatest strengths. They know customers, make quick decisions and solve problems themselves. But as a business expands, this hands-on model can become difficult to sustain. When the founder becomes a bottleneck Yeo Kee Heng, known as Francis, is an MBA student at British University Vietnam (BUV) who runs a technology consulting business in Singapore with an established client base. For years, he viewed smooth daily operations as a sign of effective management. As the business grew, however, operational issues consumed more of his time, leaving less room for strategic planning. "I realized I had become good at managing the day-to-day operation, but that was different from truly leading a business. I needed to think strategically and learn how to lead change," Francis said. His experience reflects a broader challenge for founder-led businesses. When decision-making remains concentrated at the top, employees can become accustomed to waiting for approval rather than taking ownership, while the founder becomes increasingly tied to day-to-day operations. This challenge was described as an "execution gap" at SME Forum 2026, where business leaders and experts discussed the importance of organizational structures and operating systems as companies expand. Dao Gia Hung, Head of VPBank SME, said some Vietnamese businesses have grown from small companies into enterprises worth hundreds or thousands of billions of dong, while others have stalled despite similar market opportunities. "The difference is not market opportunity, but the ability to execute and adapt," he said. "Without agility and continuous innovation, businesses can easily fall behind as competition intensifies." Scaling, therefore, requires more than increasing sales or hiring employees. Founders eventually need to shift from solving problems themselves to building teams and systems that can do so independently. Growing as a leader For some business owners, management education can help with that transition. But returning to university while running a company can be difficult, making flexible and applied programs particularly relevant. British University Vietnam offers the MSc International Business Management (MIBM), targeting working professionals and business owners. The program is delivered in Vietnam over 12 months, shorter than many international master's programs that typically take around two years. Under the dual-degree program, graduates will receive master's degrees from both BUV and Manchester Metropolitan University. BUV was included in the QS Global MBA Rankings for the second consecutive year in September 2026, ranking 41st in Asia. Manchester Metropolitan University, meanwhile, has a Triple Crown-accredited business school, holding the three major international business school accreditations. The MIBM covers international business strategy, finance, operations, project management, data analytics and emerging markets. Case studies, simulations and applied projects expose students to strategic decisions relevant to business owners. International study tours offer exposure to different business environments, including developments in technology and artificial intelligence. Through BUV's network of more than 500 corporate partners, students can also meet industry experts and senior executives. "At BUV, learning does not come only from textbooks," Francis said. "We have opportunities to meet experts and senior business leaders whom we would otherwise rarely have access to and to learn directly from their experience." For SME owners, sustainable growth depends not only on how much work a founder can handle but also on whether the business can operate without constant reliance on one person. The transition requires founders to move from personally keeping the business running to building the teams, systems and strategic direction needed for further growth. Learn more about the MSc International Business Management (MIBM) here .

picked.t: Singapore homegrown restaurant brand Crystal Jade's holding firms placed under receivership
picked.body: Kroll said in a news release on Wednesday that its representatives had been appointed receivers of Crystal Jade Culinary Concepts Holding Pte Ltd and Crystal Jade Culinary Concepts Holding (Great China) Limited, which are the holding firms for the group’s restaurant operations in Singapore and Hong Kong respectively, Channel News Asia reported. A receivership typically gives an independent party control over some or all of a company’s assets, often when the company is unable to meet its financial obligations. Kroll’s representatives are examining Crystal Jade’s financial and operational affairs and evaluating strategic options for its portfolio of brands, restaurants and businesses to stabilize the group and preserve its value, the advisory firm said, adding that it would engage stakeholders on potential restructuring as and when appropriate. Kroll representatives confirmed that Crystal Jade is not exiting the food and beverage market, and the restaurant group also said its restaurants remain open, according to The Straits Times . Established in Singapore in 1991, Crystal Jade expanded over the years with multiple dining concepts both in Singapore and overseas markets, including China, South Korea and Vietnam. Its Singapore operations comprise six restaurant brands, ranging from Cantonese fine dining to casual noodle, dim sum and other Chinese cuisine concepts. Its Crystal Jade Golden Palace restaurant at The Paragon mall was awarded one Michelin star from 2016 to 2018. The group has closed five outlets in Singapore this year as part of an ongoing review of its operations and outlet network, leaving 13 outlets in the city-state. A subsidiary, Crystal Jade Fine Dining, was earlier this year charged over failing to file its complete income tax return on time without a reasonable excuse, which could result in a fine of up to S$5,000 (US$3,900) if found guilty.

picked.t: Vietnamese man trades city life for eight years alone on deserted island
picked.body: "Living alone on the island has made me happier and more fulfilled," the 51-year-old from Cua Ong Ward in Quang Ninh province. In 2017, while exploring the waters around the Co To archipelago, he stopped at Bay Sao, a cluster of seven small islands covering about one hectare in the Co To Special Administrative Zone, more than 40 km from the mainland. He was immediately captivated by its unspoiled scenery and tranquility. Each island looked different: some were covered in greenery, while white sandbars connected others at low tide. No one lived there, and piles of trash had washed ashore, yet the vegetation remained lush. Winters were warmer than on the mainland, while summer nights were cool enough to require a blanket. After returning four times that year, Hanh became increasingly determined to live there. In early 2018, after receiving permission from the authorities, he told his family about his decision. His wife objected and threatened to divorce him. "I had made sure my wife and children were financially secure. I knew she threatened divorce because she was worried, not because she truly intended to leave," he says. He had spent years abroad doing business. He sold his car, bought a motorboat, and gathered clothes, other supplies, water containers, a hoe, a knife, and a lighter before setting sail. In his early days there, he slept under a tarp on a flat stretch of land. During the day, he cast nets for fish, cleared trash from the beach and gathered bamboo and driftwood to make tables and chairs. At night, the island was pitch-black and silent except for the waves. He did not leave the place for four months. Once his shelter was relatively stable, he went back to the mainland for seedlings and brought chickens and puppies to the island. A year later, he built a sturdy hut. In 2020, he transported construction materials from the mainland, built a house and invested hundreds of millions of dong in a solar power system. With no one else around, he taught himself to handle every task, including repairing equipment damaged by the salty air. Fresh water was his greatest challenge. While walking around the island, Hanh noticed a crack in a cliff where plants grew particularly well. Suspecting an underground water source, he dug a well and found water. He now stores well water and rainwater in 200-liter containers, providing enough for his daily needs and irrigation. To grow his own food, he took lemongrass, taro, pineapple, cassava, and banana plants to the island. He gathered soil by hand, sifting it from among the rocks until he had enough to plant crops. Because the soil lacked nutrients, he collected dead shore crabs from the beach each day and buried them around the plants as fertilizer. His garden now produces a variety of vegetables. The banana plants bear fruit year-round, yielding more than he can eat. To support himself, Hanh has a permit to farm sea snails and sea cucumbers in the surrounding waters, and he also fishes. His hundreds of chickens forage for food but are supplemented with feed brought from the mainland. His more than 30 dogs catch fish and occasionally eat rice scraps he gives them. "I live alone, but I’m not afraid or sad. I simply enjoy it," he says. During his second summer there, Hanh’s wife spent two weeks on Bay Sao and gradually accepted his decision. Once his life had become stable, he reconnected with close friends. Some occasionally visit and bring supplies, but no one has stayed longer than two weeks. Island life also brings weather-related risks. Hanh returns to the mainland for shelter before major storms. Super Typhoon Yagi swept through in 2024, toppling trees, tearing the roof of his house and sending his animals running in all directions. He later spent several months repairing the damage. The hardest part remains the isolation. For days at a time, the only sounds are the waves and his animals. Some visitors tell him his life looks comfortable, but all have declined his invitation to stay for a month because they cannot tolerate the isolation, he says. Hanh now returns to the mainland for a few days every month or two before heading back to Bay Sao. Recently, his older brother and nephew have occasionally joined him to help fish and care for the animals. After eight years, Hanh feels healthier and more relaxed. Even so, he does not advise others to follow his way of life. "Everyone has their own definition of happiness and different living circumstances." Hanh plans to remain on Bay Sao for as long as his health allows. Senior Lt. Tran Quang Thanh, the police officer responsible for Dong Tien Hamlet in the Co To Special Administrative Zone, says Hanh moved to Bay Sao after winning a tender to develop a marine business there. The regular presence of residents on outlying islands helps maintain security and protect national sovereignty, he adds. picked.t: Vietnam records nearly 15% rise in foreign tourists as Southeast Asian countries suffer tourism decline
picked.body: Mainland China remained Vietnam's largest source market, with 3.95 million visitors, accounting for about 22.3% of the total. South Korea ranked second with approximately 3.05 million visitors, or 17.3%. Russia ranked third with 1.1 million, followed by Taiwan (964,000) and the U.S. (746,000), according to the General Statistics Office. The rest of the top 10 were Cambodia (688,000), Japan (674,000), India (670,000), the Philippines (522,000) and Australia (485,000). In September, foreign visitors declined by 11.3% from August but rose by 16.5% year-on-year to 1.77 million. Martin Koerner, commercial director of The Anam Group, a chain of luxury resort hotels in Vietnam, said what is particularly encouraging is Vietnam's diversification of source markets. European arrivals increased by more than 50%, while arrivals from markets including the United States, Australia and India also recorded strong growth. This makes Vietnam less dependent on only one or two major Asian source markets, he added. "Vietnam is no longer seen simply as an inexpensive holiday destination. Increasingly, it is being recognized as a destination capable of delivering sophisticated, world-class hospitality," Koerner said. Several Southeast Asian countries have faced declines in international arrivals amid the impact of the Middle East crisis. Thailand received 22.6 million international visitors from January to September, down 3.65% year-on-year, while Singapore recorded 11.43 million in the first eight months, a 1.7% decline from a year earlier. Just over 2 million international tourists visited Cambodia during the first eight months of 2026, down nearly half from the same period last year, The Phnom Penh Post reported.

picked.t: Ho Chi Minh City named world's second best coffee destination
picked.body: The city scored 66.8 points in the 2026 Holafly Coffee Travel Index, ranking behind Colombia's Eje Cafetero coffee region, which topped the list with 71.4 points. Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, ranked third with 64.1 points. Holafly assessed 18 coffee destinations worldwide across five categories: coffee origin heritage, cafe density, coffee tourism infrastructure, specialty coffee affordability and global demand. Each category accounted for 20% of the overall score. It described the index as a guide for travelers interested in combining coffee experiences with tourism. For visitors to Ho Chi Minh City, the report suggests the city's appeal lies not only in the price of its coffee but also in the variety of experiences available, from traditional sidewalk stalls to contemporary specialty cafes. "The contrast here is what makes exploring so fun: you can sip a strong brew sitting on a tiny plastic stool at a sidewalk stall, then walk two blocks to a quiet, air-conditioned third-wave roaster," it said. A specialty pour-over coffee or traditional sweet iced coffee costs around $2 on average, it added. Vietnam's distinctive Robusta beans were also cited as a key factor behind the city's high ranking. The country is the largest exporter of Robusta coffee in the world, accounting for about 40% of the global market share, according to official sources. One of the defining features of Ho Chi Minh City's coffee culture is ca phe sua da . Made with strong, dark-roasted coffee traditionally brewed through a filter and mixed with sweetened condensed milk before being poured over ice, the drink is closely associated with the city's vibrant sidewalk cafe culture. From plastic stools on busy streets to modern specialty coffee shops, the signature drink remains a popular choice among both locals and visitors. Colombia's Eje Cafetero took the top spot with 71.4 points, helped by its coffee-growing heritage, farm tourism opportunities and affordability. A specialty coffee in the region costs around $1.50 on average, according to Holafly. Addis Ababa followed HCMC with 64.1 points. The Ethiopian capital was highlighted for its connection to the origins of Arabica coffee, traditional coffee ceremonies and low prices, with single-origin cups averaging around $1.20. Melbourne ranked fourth with 62.5 points, followed by Rome at 58.9, Brazil's Minas Gerais at 57.3, Antigua in Guatemala at 54.2, Havana at 52.8, Kigali at 49.1, and Yemen's Sana'a and Haraz region at 46.5.
